quotes.text: The modern central bank is therefore the product of a long historical process.

fragments.text: On one hand lies the Montesquieu tradition, concerned with limiting arbitrary power through institutional checks.
On the other lies the tradition of Locke and Hume, concerned with establishing money and credit as public goods upon which society depends.

summary.text: The speaker says modern central banks combine institutional checks on arbitrary power with money and credit as public goods upon which society depends.

fragments.text: Modern independent central banks are not independent of democratic government in the important sense that their authority originates in legislation or the like enacted by elected representatives.
In the Bank of England’s case, Parliament defines the objectives, establishes the powers, and retains the authority to amend the framework within which we operate.

summary.text: The speaker says modern independent central banks are not independent of democratic government, and Parliament defines the Bank of England’s objectives and establishes its powers.

fragments.text: One version of the criticism is that the central bank remains too close to financial interests.

summary.text: The speaker says critics argue central banks are too close to financial interests, while financial interests argue that regulation has gone too far.

fragments.text: Central banks cannot take legitimacy for granted. They must explain their decisions clearly.
